engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Middlegame: Piece Coordination
chess.body: Good chess is about all your pieces working together. Ask: which of my pieces is worst placed? Improve it. A knight on the rim is dim (a1, h1 etc). A bishop blocked by its own pawns is a 'tall pawn.' Rooks need open files. Queen needs safety. Coordinate: every piece pointing at the same sector = overwhelming attack.

wisdom.title: Wisdom from Fathers Before You
wisdom.body: Your father had flaws. His father did too. But they also gave you things you don't yet see. The goal isn't to be a perfect father — it's to be a slightly more conscious one. Break the patterns you don't want to pass on. Keep the ones that built you. Each generation improves a little. That's legacy.

book.author: Stephen Covey
book.chapter: Habit 4: Think Win-Win or No Deal
book.lesson: Most people operate from scarcity — if you win, I lose. Win-win thinking comes from an abundance mentality: there is enough for everyone, and cooperation creates more value than competition. Covey's most important corollary: 'or No Deal.' If a genuine win-win solution cannot be found, the integrity move is to agree not to deal. Not every partnership, transaction, or negotiation should happen. The willingness to walk away from a bad deal is what makes you trustworthy in good ones. People who always find a way to close the deal always find a way to disadvantage one party.
book.key_quote: Win-win is not compromise. It's a creative solution where both parties genuinely benefit.
book.action: In your next negotiation or conflict, explicitly ask: 'what does the other person actually need here?' Then find a solution that addresses both needs.
crux: Character ethic beats personality ethic. Techniques without character are manipulation.
Paradigms determine what you see. Change the map before optimising the route.
Habit 1 — Be Proactive: between stimulus and response is your freedom to choose.
Focus on your Circle of Influence, not your Circle of Concern. The first grows; the second drains.
Habit 2 — Begin with the End in Mind: write the personal mission statement, then live backwards from it.
Habit 3 — First Things First: Quadrant II (important, not urgent) is where effectiveness lives.
Urgency addiction disguises itself as productivity. Most of Quadrant I is neglected Quadrant II.
Habit 4 — Think Win/Win: scarcity thinking produces win/lose; abundance produces cooperation.
Habit 5 — Seek First to Understand, Then to Be Understood. Diagnose before prescribing.
Empathic listening is the highest-leverage communication skill and almost nobody does it.
Habit 6 — Synergise: 1+1 can equal 3 when differences are valued rather than tolerated.
Habit 7 — Sharpen the Saw: renew physical, mental, social/emotional, spiritual capacity.
P/PC balance: production versus production capability. Killing the goose for the eggs.
The Emotional Bank Account — trust accumulates through deposits and is spent by withdrawals.
learnings: Effectiveness is a private victory before it is a public one.
Quadrant II work never announces itself. You must schedule it.
Most communication failures are prescription before diagnosis.
Renewal is not a reward for finishing. It is the capacity to finish.
examples: Viktor Frankl in the camps: everything removed except the choice of response. The origin of Habit 1.
Covey's funeral exercise — what four speakers would say about you — reframes goals from achievement to character.
The father who lists his son's faults and cannot understand why the son won't talk. Diagnosis skipped entirely.
adapt: Circle of influence on the Meta case: control the caption process, not the platform's decision.
Quadrant II: the Dubai applications and the daughter's bedtime. Neither is urgent. Both decide the decade.
Sharpen the saw is not optional at 7 hours' sleep — it is what makes the analysis correct.
Emotional bank account at home: presence deposits daily. The balance is what carries the hard months.

interview_tech.q: How do you evaluate a capex request for store refurbishment versus a new store?
interview_tech.a: Both need incremental cash flow, but the counterfactual differs. For a new store, the baseline is zero. For a refurbishment, the baseline is the store's declining trajectory without investment — so the benefit is the uplift over that decline, not over today. People systematically overstate refurbishment returns by comparing post-refit sales to pre-refit sales, which double-counts the natural trend and any category resets. Ask for the do-nothing case in writing.

interview_tech.q: What is the one number you would put on a retail CEO's daily dashboard?
interview_tech.a: Like-for-like sales versus plan, with gross margin rate alongside it. One without the other is dangerous — sales up on margin collapse is a discount habit forming, and margin up on sales collapse is a range problem. If forced to a single figure, gross profit versus plan, because it moves only when something real happens. Everything else — footfall, conversion, basket, density — is diagnostic detail you reach for once that number moves.

interview_soft.q: What do you know about our company?
interview_soft.a: The disqualifying answer is anything from the homepage. Come with: their last reported results and one number from them, their format or brand mix and how it differs from peers, one strategic move in the last 18 months, and one question you genuinely cannot answer from outside. For a Gulf retail group that means knowing their franchise portfolio, which markets they operate directly versus through partners, and their exposure to mall footfall.

interview_soft.q: How do you build credibility in the first 90 days in a new company?
interview_soft.a: Deliver one visible thing early and be accurate about everything. Concretely: get the close done cleanly, learn the actual business by walking the stores rather than reading the reports, and find the one number everyone argues about and fix its definition. Do not restructure anything in the first quarter. Credibility in finance is cumulative and fragile — it comes from being right repeatedly, not from an early bold move.

cfo_field.q: The offer is decided by the non-technical questions.
cfo_field.a: Everyone shortlisted can do the technical work — that is why they were shortlisted. What separates the offer is whether the panel believes you can hold a room, disagree with a CEO without theatre, and be trusted with bad news. Prepare the failure story properly: what you decided, what it cost, what you changed afterwards. A candidate with no failure story reads as someone who has never owned a decision.

cfo_field.q: A forecast that is never wrong is a forecast nobody is using.
cfo_field.a: Track forecast accuracy as a metric in its own right — absolute percentage error by month, by category. Under 5% at group level is good in retail; over 15% and the business has stopped believing you. But an FP&A team that is never wrong is sandbagging, and sandbagging is more expensive than error: it prices in a buffer everyone plans around, and the buffer compounds up the hierarchy.

lichess_summary.session_summary: AKK_010’s 0‑2 record shows a total collapse in opening preparation—your current repertoire yields no wins and leaves you vulnerable from move 1, so ditch the current “weakest opening” and replace it with a solid, theory‑tested line (e.g., 1.e4 c5 Saemisch or 1.d4 Nf6 Catalan) that forces your opponent out of their comfort zone. Your play lacks strategic depth: you’re losing material early and failing to coordinate pieces, so adopt a strict “no‑pawn‑grab” rule for the first 10 moves and practice basic endgame drills to solidify conversion skills. From now on, schedule three focused training sessions per week—one on opening theory, one on tactical pattern recognition, and one on endgame fundamentals—and review each loss with a computer engine to pinpoint the exact move that cost you the game; only then will you stop being a statistical dead weight.
